clue.text: In turn, decline answer for one such as Liszt

indicators.note: turning here means the pieces that follow are read from right to left

parts.note: to decline is to ebb, as a tide or fortune does

explanation.surface: Someone refuses an offer, in turn, from a figure like the composer Liszt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In turn' reverses EBBA to give the answer. The composer Franz Liszt took minor orders late in life and was known as the Abbé Liszt.
explanation.definitionFit: Liszt took minor holy orders, so he was a French-style cleric, the title used for any such churchman.

clue.text: Coming from the sun, the earth is a poor place

definitions.text: Coming from the sun, the earth
definitions.meaning: counting outward from the sun, our planet is in position number three
a developing country, the old term for poorer nations

explanation.surface: An astronomer describing Earth's position in the solar system comes to a gloomy conclusion about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is the third planet from the sun, and the phrase was long used for developing, poorer countries.

clue.text: Sir, "nett" and "net" are the same …

parts.note: the ellipsis invites the answer to complete the sentence: the two spellings match except for one extra letter T, read as a three-word phrase

explanation.surface: A pedant addressing someone as Sir points out that two spellings of a word are identical.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as BAR ONE T and it finishes the sentence: 'nett' and 'net' are the same except for one T. The title holder is addressed as 'Sir'.
explanation.definitionFit: A holder of a hereditary British title ranking below a baron is styled 'Sir' before his name.

clue.text: Prize fish at the shore

parts.note: a gar is a long-snouted freshwater fish
to land is to come ashore, and land is the shore as opposed to sea

explanation.surface: An angler wins an award for a fish caught at the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: A wreath of flowers was the traditional prize or honour awarded to a victor.

clue.text: Fear something wrong as alarms let off

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone bad or wrong, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone suspects trouble when the alarms are set off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals an anagram of ALARMS LET.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to suspect that something is amiss, as if detecting a rodent's odour.

clue.text: One-nil for United

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
nil means none

explanation.surface: A football result: a one-nil win for Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a football score with United the team; United is in fact the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Things joined together into a single whole are combined, an idiom for united.

clue.text: Emperor again resolved to free union

indicators.note: resolved in the sense of broken down and reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An emperor once more decides to liberate a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' signals an anagram of EMPEROR AGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding in which both partners agree that relations outside it are allowed is a loose, unconstrained partnership.

clue.text: Violin lessons, perhaps, for band round house

definitions.meaning: a programme of study in a stringed instrument
in architecture, a horizontal band of masonry running round a building's walls

explanation.surface: A child's violin lessons are being offered in exchange for a band to play round at someone's house.
explanation.definitionFit: Lessons on a stringed instrument form a course, and the architectural term names a projecting horizontal masonry band.

clue.text: A note about my source of oak

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first pair of letters is placed round the next piece

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

explanation.surface: A remark about the origin of an oak tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts COR inside AN. COR is a British cry of surprise, matching 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oak tree grows from the nut it drops, so the nut is the tree's origin.

clue.text: Legally obliged person on right to follow short figure

indicators.note: the right-wing person comes after the shortened figure
short means cut, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a statue is a carved or cast figure
a Tory is a British Conservative, a party on the political right

explanation.surface: Someone politically right-wing is forced by law to walk behind a short person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' drops the last letter of the figure; 'to follow' puts the right-winger after it. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Something required by statute law is mandatory, so a person bound by it is under that compulsion.

clue.text: In painting, record me turning to this?

definitions.text: In painting, record me turning to this?

indicators.note: turning means the whole assembled string is read from right to left
in places the record and me inside the painting word

parts.note: painting is art
an EP is an extended-play record
taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist wonders whether to take up a particular painting medium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts EPME inside ART to give AREPMET; 'turning' reverses that. The whole clue also reads as an artist asking whether to switch to this medium.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a painting medium in which pigment is bound with egg yolk, used before oils.

clue.text: Succeed as priest filling vessel

indicators.note: filling means the priest goes inside the vessel

parts.note: a pail is a bucket, a vessel
Rev is short for Reverend, a priest's title

explanation.surface: A clergyman squeezes into a bucket and succeeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' puts the priest's title inside the bucket; 'vessel' tempts as a ship but is a container here.
explanation.definitionFit: To win through or triumph is to come out on top, a synonym of succeed.

clue.text: Plant one left in wind

indicators.note: in means the two letters go inside the wind

parts.note: an easterly is a wind from the east
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: One plant is left out in the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts IL inside EASTERLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A white trumpet-flowered lily traditionally used to decorate churches in spring is a plant.

clue.text: In Scarlet, a Study

indicators.note: in places the letter A inside the colour word

parts.note: scarlet is a shade of red

explanation.surface: A reference to the Sherlock Holmes story A Study in Scarlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts A inside RED. The surface recalls A Study in Scarlet, the first Sherlock Holmes story.
explanation.definitionFit: To study a subject, especially at university in Britain, is to read it.

clue.text: French is used in orders to restrain dangerous material

indicators.note: restraining means holding in, so the orders enclose the French word

parts.note: ASBOs were British anti-social behaviour orders, court orders restricting troublemakers
est is French for 'is'

explanation.surface: French police use court orders to restrain someone hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to restrain' puts the French word inside the orders. ASBOs were British court orders against anti-social behaviour; 'used in' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous mineral once used for insulation, it is now known to cause lung disease, so it is hazardous.

clue.text: Show embarrassment about a right being traded away

indicators.note: about means going around, so the blushing phrase surrounds the next pieces

parts.note: to show embarrassment is to be red in the face

explanation.surface: Someone blushes about having a right taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ART (A + RT) inside BE RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To swap goods for other goods without money is to exchange them, so traded away in a deal.

clue.text: One not liking mad chap to be half-hearted

indicators.note: half of the doubled middle letters is removed, so the heart is halved

parts.note: the Mad Hatter is the tea-party host in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: Someone who dislikes a crazy fellow is lukewarm about him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be half-hearted' removes one of the two central Ts from HATTER, the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who loathes or detests something is the opposite of a fan.

clue.text: Fixing that holds weight away from the centre

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the fixing word encloses the weight letter

parts.note: righting is putting right, fixing

explanation.surface: A clamp that carries a load is moved off-centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that holds' puts W inside RIGHTING.
explanation.definitionFit: In politics the conservative side is the opposite of centrist, removed from the middle ground.

clue.text: Acting as PM, following union orders?

definitions.meaning: a prime minister governs, so doing that job is ruling
industrial action in which workers obey every regulation exactly to slow things down

explanation.surface: A deputy stands in as prime minister while doing what the trade unions tell him.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a protest where staff follow regulations to the letter, while a premier's job is governing.

clue.text: Runs with each child in grounds

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a son is a child

explanation.surface: Someone runs around a park with every one of their children.
explanation.definitionFit: Grounds for something are its cause or justification, a synonym.

clue.text: Start to drink more rum, and walk unsteadily

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: rum in the British sense of strange; more rum is stranger

explanation.surface: Someone begins drinking more rum and staggers.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum here is the British adjective meaning odd, not the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: To totter or move shakily, as an old person might, is a synonym for walking unsteadily.

clue.text: Sensitive plant has no citrus smell before

parts.note: taken as written
a lime is a citrus fruit
a tang is a sharp smell
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A touchy plant lacks any lemony scent it once had.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin name means 'touch me not', given to plants whose seed pods burst at a touch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin 'touch me not' names plants such as busy Lizzie relatives that react to touch.

clue.text: To undo delete, freshly insert a couple of lines

indicators.note: freshly suggests made anew, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line, so two lines give two Ls

explanation.surface: A computer user, to reverse a deletion, puts back a few lines of text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freshly' signals an anagram of INSERT, giving REINST.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting software back after removing it reverses the deletion, so it undoes that removal.

clue.text: School's middle entrance is appropriate

indicators.note: only the middle of the school name is kept, so its outer letters go

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: A school's central entrance is fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle' strips the outer letters from HARROW, the English public school, leaving ARRO. 'Appropriate' is the verb, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to claim or take for oneself without right, which is the verb's meaning.

clue.text: Got back in the saddle and went green?

definitions.meaning: reprocessed waste for reuse, the environmentally friendly thing

explanation.surface: A rider resumed cycling and became environmentally conscious.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally cycled again, and the usual word for reprocessing waste materials in an eco-friendly way.

clue.text: Cause nervousness in deathly sound

definitions.meaning: the death ... is the noise in the throat of a dying person

explanation.surface: A ghostly noise from a dying man frightens those around him.
explanation.definitionFit: To unnerve someone is to fluster them, and the noise of a dying breath is the death sound.

clue.text: Medium in difficulty? Initially simple for solver

indicators.note: in places the medium letter inside the difficulty word

parts.note: a hole is a fix or difficulty

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A psychic medium is in trouble, but at first the puzzle seems easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside HOLE. Sherlock is the great solver of mysteries, famous for calling things elementary.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional detective of Baker Street is the archetypal solver of crimes.

clue.text: Shock an apostle by speaking

indicators.note: said out loud, the phrase gives a word with the same sound

parts.note: Paul is an apostle, so an apostle is 'a Paul'

explanation.surface: A disciple is horrified when someone speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by speaking' means the phrase 'a Paul' is said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To horrify or dismay someone is to shock them, a synonym.
